prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep B008 as a single prize part, unchanged from round 1. The round-1 exchange tested the physics and nobody disputed it: magic-wavelength trapping cancels Doppler, recoil and lattice-induced shifts while many neutral atoms are interrogated in parallel, and that is what took optical clocks from the 1e-15 regime to about 1e-18, reproduced independently in Sr, Yb and Hg. From the atomic-structure side I can say that the systematic budget (blackbody shift, lattice light shifts, hyperpolarisability) is well understood and not an artefact of one laboratory. The chair asks how to make the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes explicit without implying the SI redefinition. My answer is the citation wording itself: it names the invention, the neutral-atom optical lattice clock, and says nothing about timekeeping in general, the comb, ion control or the second. The comb is the ruler that reads out the clock and single-ion control is the technique behind ion clocks; the engineering of a magic-wavelength lattice that holds thousands of atoms in a Doppler- and recoil-free regime is neither. I regard the two-name attribution as defensible because it maps onto proposal plus first realisation (Katori) and the record accuracy and many-body operation (Ye), and the citation is worded as the invention and its development rather than the whole field. Of the alternatives, none addresses the question of distinctness better than the clock does.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is still overlap and credit. A sceptic can call the clock a very successful refinement of frequency-comb metrology and ion control, and Danielsson is right that this is the first objection the Academy would hear. I think it is answerable on the physics, but the answer rests on the committee being willing to say so in the citation and in the motivation. The second objection is attribution: PTB, SYRTE, NIST and ion-clock groups, and early lattice-clock proposals, are outside the two names, and no wording fully removes that. The third is timing, because the SI second is not yet redefined. I have concluded that this cuts both ways and should not drive the decision: the prize recognises the invention, not the redefinition, and a decision to wait for it would tie the award to a metrological process the discovery itself does not depend on. I accept that this is a judgment and not a fact.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B035 as a prediction-plus-discovery case that changes how correlated electrons are understood, and regards B008 as a large precision gain and a defensible first alternative, but the 2005 and 2012 overlap worries them.
responses.response: I take your point that the clock does not change our picture of matter in the way a new correlated platform does, but I think precision at 1e-18 is part of physics itself and not only engineering: it makes gravitational redshift measurable across millimetres and tightens bounds on varying constants. On B035 I keep the reservation you state yourself. The pairing mechanism is unsettled, Yuan Cao and other experimentalists are outside the three names, and the 2016 and 2010 prizes already touched topological phases and graphene. If the committee wants a correlated-electron theme, I would wait until the mechanism is clearer. Nothing in your statement gives me new evidence that moves it above the clock, but I agree that your concern about overlap should be dealt with in the citation and I have tried to do that.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) as an original thirty-year line, concedes that the experimental credit and the 2012 overlap are contestable, and names B008 as the more compact and less disputed prize if those points are unresolved.
responses.response: Your own statement points to the weak spot. The 2012 prize covered the foundation of ion quantum control, including the first ion gate at NIST, so the overlap argument applies to B022 at least as strongly as to B008, as the chair summary notes. For B022 the experimental allocation is also arbitrary: Blatt, Wineland's NIST group and Monroe all have claims, and a three-name limit forces a choice. For B008 the two-name attribution maps onto one invention with few omissions. I would also say that scalable quantum computing has not arrived, and a prize for the proposal and realisation would be recognised before the technology it names is demonstrated. I do not doubt the science of B022, and I would support it if the committee wanted a quantum-information prize, but I do not see it surpassing the clock this year.

responses.point: Johansson moved B008 to first place after the first round, keeps B012 as first alternative, and notes the clock's credit is a judgment and not a fact because of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and ion-clock contributions.
responses.response: I agree with your account of why circuit QED is harder to argue than the clock this year: strong coupling is distinct from the macroscopic tunnelling of 2025, but a second circuit prize so soon, with Girvin and Huang outside the names, would be difficult to defend. I would also add to your credit point that the committee can narrow the wording to the invention and its development, as the citation does, and say plainly in the motivation that other groups pushed the field. I do not think the omitted contributors justify a third name, because that would require us to define the clock community, which has no natural boundary at three.

responses.point: Kroll supports B008, discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and work in laser stabilisation in the same technical area, and has not found any two-part prize stronger than the clock alone.
responses.response: I agree with your conclusion that no pairing with another shortlisted entry is stronger than the clock alone, and I would keep to one part. Your disclosure matters for the earlier-prize question: since you know the comb and ultrastable-laser technology closely, your view that the lattice itself, and not the laser, is the new element is useful, and I accept it. I would not add comb or laser-stabilisation names to cover the ecosystem, since that is exactly what the 2005 prize recognised. A recusal is for the committee to decide, but your disclosed tie is to Hall, not to Katori or Ye, so I would not require it.

responses.point: Olsson presses for the citation to say plainly that the prize is for the invention and its realisation at extreme accuracy and not for all optical clocks, and discloses field proximity to B009.
responses.response: I accept that and it is reflected in the citation I now propose: it names the optical lattice clock and its development, with no reference to optical clocks in general or to the second. I would be willing to put in the motivation that the NIST, PTB, SYRTE and ion-clock groups also contributed. On B009, I still rank it as my first alternative because Rose, Haider and Urban form a natural three-person split, but your own disclosure and the Krivanek question are real, and I would not want it used as the second part of a two-part prize.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the objection a sceptical Academy member would raise first, and will not accept a configuration that widens credit to comb or laser contributors.
responses.response: I agree with both points and I have moved toward your position on how to answer. It is not enough to call overlap a framing matter: the citation and motivation should say what is new, which is Doppler- and recoil-free parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength. I also agree that widening credit to comb or ultrastable-laser people is the wrong remedy. On B056, I respect that the Higgs observation is arguably the bigger scientific event, but the four-name credit across ATLAS and CMS forces an arbitrary choice at the three-name limit, and I do not think that should be solved by adding it as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize on the strength of the citation wording alone.
Exact priority between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations, and the weight of other groups' contributions, which I cannot verify from the supplied files.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI redefinition of the second; I think it should not delay an award for the invention but I cannot exclude that others will.
I judge the atomic-structure side of the clock better than the experimental engineering, so my confidence on the stability budget is higher than on the practical comparison between laboratories.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or their groups; my collaborations (Anne L'Huillier, the Lund and ETH Zurich attosecond groups, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) concern attosecond photoionisation and highly charged ions, not the lattice clock. I have noted the disclosures of Kroll (Hall's laboratory), Olsson (B009), Johansson (B012), Eriksson (B035) and Pearce (B042) and do not think any of them requires recusal from a B008 vote. I remain a theorist and treat the experimental engineering with corresponding care.
